title: The Questions That Turn Messy Problems into Clear Ones
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Andrea Chiarelli draws on Lindsay and Bawden's Pig Wrestling to argue that leaders get stuck on messy problems because they keep stepping into the pen, engaging with assumption and ego rather than cleaning the problem first. She offers three questions as cleaning tools. What am I really wrestling with? separates fact from interpretation, When does this not happen? replaces blame with evidence through exceptions and positive deviance, and What would I like to see instead? shifts from fixing to designing a concrete future. Throughout she positions curiosity as the leader's discipline, since every question carries a frame about what is relevant and what success means. The close is that curiosity does not solve the mess but points to the part that can be cleaned.
points: Most stuck problems persist because leaders are solving the wrong version of them.
Separating observable facts from attached interpretations shrinks a problem to something behavioural.
Asking when a problem does not happen surfaces exceptions that point to workable conditions.
The miracle-style question forces a concrete vision, not a slogan like better collaboration.
Questions design reality because each one chooses a frame, and so shapes the organisation a leader builds.
quotes: Their insight is deceptively simple: most problems stay stuck because we’re solving the wrong version of them. An important skill you can develop is to clean the problem first: to strip it back until you can see what’s actually happening.
This question invites you to separate fact from interpretation. Facts are what anyone could observe. Interpretations are the meanings you’ve attached to those facts.

This is the question that transforms blame into insight. Most of us default to asking why: “Why do they resist change?” or “Why does communication break down?” But “why” questions tend to invite justification and speculation.
It’s a deceptively powerful exercise. You can’t answer it with abstractions. For example, answering “Better collaboration” doesn’t work: that’s a slogan, not a vision.

Leaders often equate authority with having answers. But the reality is that questions design reality. Every question presupposes a frame: what counts as relevant, what success means, where agency sits.
